where: Section 1, paragraph after the Holevo bound
problem: "Equality is possible in the limit of many copies for some channels" is misleading. The Holevo bound is reached asymptotically for product signal states with collective (joint) measurements on the outputs — this is the achievability part of the HSW theorem and holds for every channel, not only some. As written, a student may conclude most channels never reach χ.
fix: "Equality is possible in the limit of many copies: with product signal states and joint measurements on the outputs, the rate χ (maximized over input ensembles) is achievable for any channel. For one use, I(X:Y) is generally strictly below χ."

where: Section 1 formula note and Quiz Q1 answer
problem: χ is described as "the Holevo quantity in bits per channel use". For an ensemble {px, ρx} on its own, χ is just a number of bits. It becomes bits per channel use only when ρx are the outputs of one use of a channel.
fix: Say "χ is the Holevo quantity in bits; when ρx are the outputs of one channel use, χ is in bits per channel use" — and in Q1 accept "bits" for the bare ensemble definition.

problem: The bit-flip paragraph ends by saying χ equals the capacity of a binary symmetric channel, but the depolarizing paragraph gives χ = 1 − H₂(p/2) without saying it is only the one-use value for those two inputs. A reader may carry over the capacity reading by analogy, which is not justified here.
fix: Add: "This 1 − H₂(p/2) is the χ of this two-state ensemble for one use; the full capacity comes only from the regularized limit, and larger input alphabets are allowed there."

problem: The note "χ = 0.531 bits" sits on the channel block, which suggests χ is a property of the channel alone. χ depends on the input ensemble as well as the channel.
fix: Put the note as "χ = 0.531 bits (for |0⟩, |1⟩ with p = 0.1)" or move it into the caption wording so it is tied to the ensemble.

problem: "limn→∞ (1/n)" is ambiguous on a phone screen; a student can read it as a product or as lim of n only.
fix: Write it as lim (n→∞) (1/n) χmax(N⊗n), with the same form repeated in Quiz Q7.
